reasons: Rate limits are in memory and may reset on restart or not be shared between servers, which is likely.

terms.meaning: a slow method for turning a password into a hash
a cap on how many attempts are allowed in a time window
learning secret information by measuring how long replies take

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and file purpose
sections.what: Brings in the hashing library, the rate limiter, the error type and the database calls. The file states that password hashes never leave this module.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps hashing and sign-in checks in one place.

sections.name: limits
sections.title: Attempt limits
sections.what: Sets the limits: 10 sign-in tries per email and 30 per network address in 15 minutes, and 5 sign-ups per network address per hour.
sections.why: Likely reason: slows down password guessing and mass account creation.
sections.watch_out: The limits are held in memory, so they reset on restart and are likely not shared across several servers.

sections.name: dummyHash
sections.title: Dummy hash for timing
sections.what: Creates one fake password hash the first time it is needed and reuses it. It is checked when an email is unknown, so the reply takes about as long as a real check.
sections.why: Likely reason: stops attackers learning which emails have accounts from reply speed.
sections.watch_out: It uses the same hashing cost as sign-up, so the two must stay matched.

sections.name: register
sections.title: Creating an account
sections.what: Checks the sign-up limit for the network address, hashes the password, saves the user and records when the age was confirmed. A duplicate email gives a deliberately vague message.
sections.why: Likely reason: the vague message stops people learning which emails are registered.
sections.watch_out: The email is trusted as already cleaned, so callers must run the input rules first.

sections.name: verifyCredentials
sections.title: Checking a sign-in
sections.what: Cleans the email, counts the attempt against both the email and the network address, refuses if either is over its limit, and compares the password. Success clears the email counter.
sections.why: Likely reason: counting before checking means every attempt counts, including wrong guesses.
sections.watch_out: The network counter is not cleared on success, so a busy shared network can be blocked sooner.

summary: Handles sign-up and sign-in checks, with limits on attempts.
purpose: Core rules for creating accounts and checking passwords.
why: Likely reason: hashing, attempt limits and vague error messages protect accounts from guessing and enumeration.
how: 1. Sign-up: apply the network limit, hash the password, save the user, and turn a duplicate email into a vague message. 2. Sign-in: clean the email, count the attempt, look up the user, compare with the stored hash or a dummy hash, and clear the email counter on success.
inputs: Name, email, password, network address, and the age confirmation.
outputs: A new user ID, a user record, null for wrong details, or a rate limit error.
risks: Limits are kept in memory. The network counter is not cleared on success, so shared networks hit the limit sooner.
debug: If sign-in always fails, check the hash comparison and email cleaning. If users are locked out, check the limit counters.
